base-rates-and-false-positives.guess answer: If the test is 99% accurate, a positive means I'm about 99% likely to be sick.
base-rates-and-false-positives.anchor answer: Not automatically. About 100 false alarms against only 10 real cases means most positives are wrong.
base-rates-and-false-positives.rule because: healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones
base-rates-and-false-positives.why answer: Because a positive can come from a sick person the test catches or a healthy person it mislabels, and when sick people are rare the mislabeled healthy ones outnumber them.
base-rates-and-false-positives.draw rule: Chance a positive is real = true positives / all positives
base-rates-and-false-positives.draw notes: sick people the test catches, plus healthy people it wrongly flags, both feed the positives
base-rates-and-false-positives.neighbor answer: Sensitivity is how often sick people test positive; whether a positive is real also depends on how many healthy people get false alarms.
base-rates-and-false-positives.transfer answer: A smoke alarm in a kitchen: most beeps are burnt toast, not fires, because real fires are rare and toast happens every day.

derivative.guess answer: The derivative is how much a function changes overall.
derivative.rule When: you shrink the interval around one moment
derivative.rule then: the average rate settles on the speed right then
derivative.rule because: the derivative is the local rate, not the total change
derivative.why answer: Because the derivative only looks at a tiny interval right around the moment, so a shrinking window shows the local rate.
derivative.draw rule: Derivative = the limit of change in output over change in input as the interval shrinks
derivative.draw notes: shrink the interval, and the average rate turns into the rate at one point
